exam: What clinical features differentiate pityriasis rosea from guttate psoriasis? — Look for a single herald patch, Christmas‑tree distribution, and lack of silvery scale.
A child presents with a herald patch followed by a rash; KOH is negative. What is your next step? — Reassure, provide symptomatic treatment, and arrange follow‑up; biopsy only if atypical.
How would you manage severe pruritus in a child with pityriasis rosea? — Use a low‑potency topical steroid plus an oral antihistamine; avoid systemic steroids unless complications arise.
When is it appropriate to order an HIV test in a child with pityriasis rosea? — When risk factors exist or the rash is atypical, extensive, or refractory to usual care.
What red‑flag sign would prompt urgent referral? — Development of secondary bacterial infection with fever or signs of systemic illness.
Why are systemic corticosteroids generally avoided in pityriasis rosea? — They do not alter disease course and increase risk of side effects and secondary infection.
Explain the ‘Christmas‑tree’ pattern and its diagnostic value. — Lesions align along skin tension lines on the trunk, creating a linear, symmetrical appearance characteristic of PR.
If a skin biopsy is performed, what histological finding supports pityriasis rosea? — Mild spongiosis with a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and focal parakeratosis.
ai.title: Pityriasis Rosea
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Pityriasis rosea is a self‑limited papulosquamous eruption common in children, often following a viral prodrome. Diagnosis is clinical, based on characteristic lesions and distribution.

b: Clinical diagnosis; skin biopsy rarely needed
Typical distribution: trunk and proximal limbs, sparing face
Lesions are oval, pink‑to‑brown, with a collarette of scale
sections.p: An acute, self‑limited skin eruption that begins with a single herald patch followed by a secondary eruption of smaller lesions along skin tension lines.

b: Mild: <30% body surface area, tolerable itch
Moderate: 30–60% BSA, sleep disturbance
Severe: >60% BSA, severe itch, secondary infection
sections.p: Most cases are mild and resolve in 6–8 weeks. Severe disease is defined by extensive involvement, intense pruritus, or atypical features.

b: Viral reactivation (HHV‑6/7) – most common
Recent upper‑respiratory infection – frequent trigger
Stress, seasonal change – possible contributors
In low‑resource settings consider co‑infection with HIV (atypical rash) or malaria (fever confounding picture)
sections.p: Exact cause unknown; most evidence points to reactivation of human herpesvirus‑6 or ‑7, especially in tropical settings where viral infections are common.

b: Herald patch: solitary, round, slightly raised, fine scale
Secondary lesions: multiple, same orientation, often on trunk
Mild to moderate pruritus; lesions may be asymptomatic
Rare systemic symptoms: low‑grade fever, malaise
sections.p: Begins with a solitary herald patch (2–5 cm) on the trunk, then 1–2 weeks later a symmetric eruption of 10–30 mm oval plaques following the “Christmas‑tree” pattern.
Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for atypical cases or to rule out mimics.

t.b: Rule out fungal infection when scaling is heavy — negative result supports PR

t.a: Rapid HIV test (if risk factors present)
t.b: Identify HIV‑associated atypical rash — positive result prompts broader work‑up
Elevated white count suggests bacterial superinfection — treat accordingly

b: Secondary bacterial infection (impetigo, cellulitis) – look for crusting, pus, fever
Severe pruritus causing excoriation and skin breakdown
Atypical presentation in immunocompromised child – consider alternative diagnoses
sections.p: Complications are uncommon but can be serious if missed.

b: Gentle skin emollients to reduce dryness
Topical corticosteroid (low‑potency) for intense itch – avoids systemic side effects
Oral antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine) for nocturnal pruritus – safe in children
Antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection confirmed
sections.p: Supportive care is mainstay; treat symptoms and prevent secondary infection.

Educate on avoiding scratching and maintaining skin hygiene
No vaccine or prophylaxis; recurrence is rare
sections.p: Reassure patient and family; schedule review if lesions persist beyond 8 weeks or complications develop.
